title: Why does [10, 9, 1].sort() return [1, 10, 9] in JavaScript?
explanation: Array.prototype.sort() coerces elements to strings and compares them lexicographically unless you pass a comparator. "10" sorts before "9" because "1" < "9". Always pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers.

title: Why is typeof null "object" in JavaScript?
explanation: typeof null is "object" — a bug from the first JavaScript implementation that can never be fixed without breaking the web. And NaN is a numeric value, so typeof NaN is "number".

title: Why does setTimeout inside a var loop log 3 3 3?
explanation: var is function-scoped, so all three callbacks close over the same binding. By the time the timers fire, the loop has finished and i is 3. Swap var for let and each iteration gets its own binding, logging 0 1 2.

prompt: In what order do these log?
title: Why does a resolved promise log before setTimeout(fn, 0)?
explanation: Synchronous code runs first (A, D). Then the microtask queue drains before any macrotask, so the resolved promise callback (C) beats the setTimeout (B) even at 0ms.

title: Why does spreading an object still mutate the nested object?
explanation: Spread is a shallow copy — b.nested and a.nested point at the same object. Use structuredClone(a) for a deep copy.

title: Why is [] == false true but [] === false false?
explanation: == coerces: [] becomes "" becomes 0, and false becomes 0, so 0 == 0 is true. === compares types first, and an array is never a boolean, so it's false.

prompt: After clicking once, what is count?
title: Why does calling setCount twice only increment React state by one?
explanation: Both calls read the same `count` from the render's closure, so both compute 0 + 1. The second overwrites the first. Use the updater form — setCount(c => c + 1) — to queue on the latest value and get 2.

title: Why does Array(2).fill([]) share the same array in every slot?
explanation: fill() puts the same array reference in every slot, so both rows are literally the same array. Use Array.from({ length: 2 }, () => []) to build distinct ones.

title: Why does ["1", "7", "11"].map(parseInt) return [1, NaN, 3]?
explanation: map passes (value, index) and parseInt takes (string, radix). So you get parseInt("1", 0)=1, parseInt("7", 1)=NaN (radix 1 is invalid), and parseInt("11", 2)=3 (binary). Use .map(Number) instead.

title: Why do o[1] and o["1"] set the same object key in JavaScript?
explanation: Plain object keys are always strings, so o[1] and o["1"] are the same key — the second write just overwrites the first. A Map keeps 1 and "1" distinct.

title: Why doesn't await work inside Array.prototype.forEach?
explanation: forEach ignores the promises its callback returns, so there is nothing to await. Use a for...of loop for sequential work, or await Promise.all(ids.map(work)) for parallel.

title: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 false in JavaScript?
explanation: IEEE-754 doubles can't represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a tolerance: Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON.
